title: Ground-State Sampling Correspondence between Penalty-Based and Constrained Quantum Annealing
abstract: Quantum annealing generally samples degenerate ground states with nonuniform probabilities. This unfair sampling depends on how the driver Hamiltonian couples these states near the end of annealing. For combinatorial optimization problems with a cardinality constraint, the penalty method and constrained quantum annealing (CQA) differ in these couplings. The transverse-field driver of the penalty method does not directly couple feasible ground states, whereas the fully connected XY driver of CQA couples pairs of them related by a single spin exchange. We investigate how this difference affects ground-state sampling, using closed-system simulations of random graph bipartitioning instances together with degenerate perturbation theory. For the instances studied, the conditional ground-state distribution of penalty-based quantum annealing approaches that of CQA at sufficiently large penalties and long annealing times. This convergence can be explained by the effective Hamiltonian of penalty-based quantum annealing, in which virtual single-spin flips to infeasible states generate a second-order interaction proportional to the CQA driver projected onto the feasible ground-state manifold, which is the leading term of the effective Hamiltonian of CQA. In the numerical simulations, the Jensen--Shannon divergence between the conditional ground-state distributions of penalty-based quantum annealing and CQA decreases approximately as the inverse square of the penalty-to-objective energy ratio, consistent with the perturbative analysis. This correspondence between the effective Hamiltonians extends to equal-weight fixed-magnetization constraints under the same perturbative conditions, providing a common mechanism for sampling bias in the two implementations.
summary: This paper theoretically compares two methods—penalty-based and constrained—for enforcing hard constraints in quantum annealing for optimization problems. It demonstrates that under appropriate conditions (large penalties and long times), the sampling biases of both methods converge. This convergence is explained by showing that the effective Hamiltonian of the penalty method generates an interaction term matching the leading term of the constrained method's effective Hamiltonian.
main_problem: The paper investigates the theoretical correspondence in ground-state sampling between two methods for enforcing constraints in Quantum Annealing (QA): the penalty method and Constrained Quantum Annealing (CQA).
main_result: The conditional ground-state distribution from penalty-based QA approaches that of CQA at large penalties and long annealing times, which is explained by the effective Hamiltonian generating a second-order interaction matching the leading term of the CQA effective Hamiltonian.
method: The analysis uses degenerate perturbation theory to derive effective Hamiltonians and compares ground-state sampling biases using the Jensen-Shannon divergence.
model_or_system: The model is applied to the Graph Bipartitioning Problem (GBP), an NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem, analyzed via its associated Hamiltonians ($H_{obj}$, $H_{QA}^c$, $H_{CQA}^c$).
key_observables: Conditional ground-state distribution, Jensen-Shannon divergence ($D_{JS}$), and the matching fraction ($f_{match}$).
important_parameters: The penalty coefficient ($\mu$), the annealing time ($T$), and the ratio of penalty to objective energy ($\mu / E_{obj}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the assumption that the system follows the instantaneous ground state within the accessible subspace, and that the effective Hamiltonian analysis is valid for large penalties.
figures_summary: Figures show the JS divergence decreasing approximately as the inverse square of the penalty-to-objective energy ratio ($r^{-2}$), and the matching fraction ($f_{match}$) increasing with the penalty parameter ($r$).
paper_structure: The paper first defines the Hamiltonians for both QA and CQA for constrained optimization problems. It then uses degenerate perturbation theory to derive the effective Hamiltonians. Finally, it compares the resulting ground-state sampling distributions numerically and theoretically, showing convergence under specific conditions.
why_interesting: This work provides a deep theoretical understanding of how different physical implementations (penalty vs. direct constraint) in quantum computation converge to the same physical result, offering insight into the underlying structure of quantum annealing dynamics.
